item.title: China approves limited rare earth exports to Japan, Kyodo reports
item.description:
China has approved some rare earth exports to Japan under tightened controls, Japan's Kyodo News reported on Friday, citing a source. The development marks a potential easing of the mineral squeeze Beijing imposed on Tokyo last month, though restrictions remain firmly in place.

Reuters said it could not independently verify the report. China's Ministry of Commerce has not formally announced any loosening of its export review procedures.

item.title: UK and US sign agreement to secure critical mineral supply chains
item.description:
The United States this week convened ministers from more than 50 countries at the first-ever Critical Minerals Ministerial in Washington, unveiling sweeping initiatives to counter China's dominance over materials essential for manufacturing everything from smartphones to advanced weapons systems.

The February 4 summit saw Vice President JD Vance propose an unprecedented preferential trade bloc for critical minerals, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned what he called "unfair practices" by Beijing that have undermined competitors in the global market.

item.title: Iran calls US nuclear talks in Oman 'a good start'
item.description:
The United States and Iran engaged in indirect nuclear negotiations in Muscat, Oman, on Friday, marking the first high-level diplomatic contact between the two adversaries since American airstrikes targeted Iranian nuclear facilities during the June 2025 conflict with Israel.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the talks as "a good start" and confirmed both sides agreed to continue negotiations, though significant differences remain over the scope of the discussions. The Oman-mediated talks stretched for more than five hours, with Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi shuttling between the delegations at his residence in the Omani capital.

item.title: Russian intelligence general shot in Moscow assassination attempt
item.description:
Lieutenant General Vladimir Alekseyev, the deputy chief of Russia's military intelligence agency (GRU), was shot multiple times outside a residential building in Moscow on Friday, according to Russia's Investigative Committee. The general was rushed to a hospital, while the gunman escaped the scene.

The shooting occurred on Volokolamskoe Highway in northwest Moscow, according to Russian state media. An Investigative Committee spokesperson, Svetlana Petrenko, confirmed that Alekseyev was struck multiple times by an unidentified assailant but did not provide details on his condition or name any suspects.

item.title: Big Tech plans $650B AI spending spree as investors grow wary
item.description:
America's four largest technology companies have collectively committed to spending approximately $650 billion in capital expenditures this year, marking a dramatic escalation of the artificial intelligence infrastructure race that has left investors questioning whether such massive outlays will ever pay off.

Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft have announced spending plans representing roughly a 60% increase from their combined $410 billion in 2025, according to Bloomberg data. The announcements, delivered over the past two weeks during quarterly earnings reports, triggered a sharp selloff that wiped more than $1 trillion from Big Tech market capitalizations.

item.title: DOJ's Epstein files release sparks political fallout in India
item.description:
The U.S. Department of Justice's massive release of Jeffrey Epstein documents has sparked political controversy in India, as files containing more than 3 million pages reveal the convicted sex offender's attempts to connect with some of the country's most prominent figures—though none have been linked to criminal wrongdoing.

The tranche, released on January 30 under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, shows emails, calendars, and messages that mention Indian industrialist Anil Ambani, Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri, wellness author Deepak Chopra, and several Bollywood filmmakers.

item.title: Polar vortex collapse forecast to push Arctic air into U.S. and Europe
item.description:
A persistent cold snap that has gripped the eastern United States in recent weeks is connected to the same human-induced climate change that is shrinking Arctic ice to record lows, according to leading scientists who warn such extreme weather events will intensify without significant cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.

The prolonged January and February cold outbreak, marked by record-breaking temperatures and deadly winter storms, may seem counterintuitive amid a warming planet. But atmospheric scientists say rapid Arctic warming is fundamentally reshaping weather patterns in ways that can unleash severe cold on the lower latitudes.

item.title: Epstein files trigger global resignations, criminal probes
item.description: The release of more than three million documents related to Jeffrey Epstein by the U.S. Justice Department has set off an international reckoning, as prominent figures across multiple continents face resignations, investigations, and calls for accountability over their ties to the late convicted sex offender.

item.title: Zelenskyy dismisses Russia's demand for Donbas recognition
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sharply dismissed Russia's new demand that other countries recognize the temporarily occupied Donbas region as Russian territory, declaring during a press conference with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Kyiv on February 5 that such recognition would achieve nothing and that "there is the President of Ukraine who signs documents" concerning the country's land.

The rebuke came as details emerged from the second round of US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi, where Kremlin-affiliated media outlets reported that Moscow was seeking international recognition of the eastern Ukrainian territories it occupies as part of any "grand treaty" to end the war.

item.title: Musk predicts space-based AI will surpass Earth's total in 5 years
item.description:
Elon Musk this week predicted that space-based AI computing will eclipse all of Earth's computational capacity within five years, fleshing out his bold plans for a network of up to one million solar-powered satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.

In a podcast interview with Dwarkesh Patel and Stripe co-founder John Collison on Thursday, Musk said space will become the cheapest location for AI infrastructure in less than three years. "In 36 months, but probably closer to 30 months, the most economically compelling place to put AI will be space," he said. "The only place you can really scale is space."

Asked where AI will be in five years, Musk made an even more striking claim: "My prediction is we will launch and be operating every year more AI in space than the cumulative total on Earth."

item.title: Trump rejects Russia's call to extend expired nuclear treaty
item.description:
The New START treaty officially expired on February 5, 2026, leaving the United States and Russia without binding limits on their strategic nuclear arsenals for the first time in more than half a century, sparking global security concerns and renewed discussions of nuclear armament in Europe.

The landmark arms control agreement, signed in Prague in 2010 by Presidents Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, capped each side's deployed strategic nuclear warheads at 1,550 and imposed limits on delivery systems such as intercontinental ballistic missiles and heavy bombers. The treaty was extended for five years by Presidents Joe Biden and Vladimir Putin in 2021 but could not be renewed further under its provisions.

item.title: Expert warns Musk's orbital data center timeline is 'aggressive'
item.description:
Elon Musk this week announced an ambitious plan to launch up to one million solar-powered satellites into orbit to serve as data centers for artificial intelligence, a proposal experts say faces enormous technical, financial, and environmental hurdles despite the billionaire's track record of disrupting industries.

The plan, detailed in a filing submitted to the Federal Communications Commission on January 30, came alongside the merger of SpaceX and Musk's AI venture xAI in a deal valued at $1.25 trillion. Musk has argued that Earth-based solutions cannot keep pace with AI's surging energy demands and that orbital infrastructure offers near-constant solar power without atmospheric interference.

item.title: Venezuela's political prisoners could be freed by next Friday
item.description:
Venezuela's National Assembly is on track to grant final approval to an amnesty law on Tuesday that could lead to the release of all political prisoners by February 13, according to Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez.

In a video shared on Telegram on Friday, Rodriguez announced that the Amnesty Law for Democratic Coexistence, which passed its first vote unanimously on Thursday, is expected to receive final approval next week. "We are optimistic that by next Tuesday or by Friday at the latest, everyone will be released," Rodriguez said.

The legislation, proposed by interim President Delcy Rodriguez following the U.S. military capture of Nicolas Maduro on January 3, would grant clemency to those jailed for participating in political protests or criticizing public officials. It also would lift political candidacy bans on opposition figures, including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado, return seized assets, and cancel Interpol notices to allow exiles to return home.

item.title: Satellite images show Iran prioritizing missile repairs over nuclear sites
item.description:
New satellite imagery analyzed by the New York Times shows Iran has swiftly restored more than a dozen ballistic missile facilities damaged during last year's 12-day war with Israel and subsequent U.S. strikes, while making only limited progress at major nuclear sites that were targeted in June 2025.

The finding, published Friday, coincided with the first round of indirect U.S.-Iran nuclear talks in Oman since the conflict, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi describing the negotiations as "a good start" focused "exclusively" on the nuclear issue.

item.title: US and Russia agree new nuclear talks needed after treaty expires
item.description:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared on Friday that any future nuclear arms control agreement must include China, announcing the Trump administration would not pursue a new bilateral deal with Russia following the expiration of the New START treaty.

In an essay published on the State Department's Substack page, Rubio argued that China's "rapid and opaque" nuclear buildup has rendered Cold War-era arms control models "obsolete." The announcement comes as the first time in more than half a century that the world's two largest nuclear arsenals have no legally binding limits.

item.title: Mexico to send humanitarian aid to Cuba by Monday
item.description:
As rolling blackouts leave millions of Cubans without power and public buses grind to a halt, the United States is intensifying its pressure campaign on the island nation with executive actions targeting its already dwindling fuel supplies.

President Donald Trump's January 29 executive order declared Cuba an "unusual and extraordinary threat" to U.S. national security, authorizing tariffs on imports from any country that supplies oil to the Caribbean nation. The move has effectively severed Cuba from its remaining energy lifelines, compounding a humanitarian crisis that the United Nations warned could lead to outright "collapse."

item.title: Mexico to send humanitarian aid to Cuba by Monday
item.description:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Friday that her government will dispatch humanitarian aid to Cuba by Monday, offering food and basic supplies while diplomatic talks continue over resuming oil shipments that were suspended under pressure from the Trump administration.

"We are planning to send this aid either this weekend or on Monday at the latest," Sheinbaum said at her daily morning press conference in Mexico City. "It primarily consists of food and other supplies they have requested."

The announcement comes as Mexico navigates a delicate diplomatic balancing act, seeking to maintain solidarity with the Cuban people while avoiding threatened tariffs from Washington. "Obviously, we do not want sanctions against Mexico, but we are in the process of dialogue and, for now, humanitarian aid will be sent," Sheinbaum stated.

item.title: Cuba adopts four-day work week amid deepening energy crisis
item.description:
Cuba announced emergency fuel-rationing measures on Friday, including a four-day work week for state companies and restrictions on fuel sales, as the island nation struggles with its worst energy crisis in years, fueled in part by President Donald Trump's executive order threatening tariffs on any country that supplies oil to Havana.

Deputy Prime Minister Oscar Perez-Oliva Fraga blamed Washington for the crisis, telling state television the government would "implement a series of decisions, first and foremost to guarantee the vitality of our country and essential services, without giving up on development."

item.title: US accuses China of secret 2020 nuclear test, monitor finds no evidence
item.description:
The United States accused China on Friday of carrying out a covert nuclear test in 2020, an allegation Beijing rejected as Washington pushed for a new arms control framework following the expiration of the last remaining nuclear treaty between the US and Russia.

Thomas DiNanno, Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, made the accusation at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, one day after the New START treaty expired, marking the first time in over fifty years that the world's two largest nuclear powers operate without binding limitations on their strategic arsenals.

item.title: Japanese researchers unveil 3D framework for green ammonia production
item.description:
Scientists in Japan and the United States have developed new approaches to convert nitrate pollution into ammonia, offering potential alternatives to the century-old Haber-Bosch process that currently accounts for roughly 2% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Researchers at Tohoku University unveiled a three-dimensional covalent organic framework, dubbed TU-82, that achieved an 88.1% Faradaic efficiency for electrochemical nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, with an ammonia yield rate of 2.87 milligrams per hour per square centimeter. The findings, published February 2 in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A, represent the first deployment of 3D COFs for this reaction, moving beyond the two-dimensional architectures that have dominated the field.
